The Intellectual Property Office of Singapore ruled in November that Real Madrid and Barcelona lost their joint bid to trademark 'El Clasico', with the decision favouring Liga Nacional de Fútbol Profesional. Principal assistant registrar Mark Lim Fung Chian noted the unusual alignment, observing that clubs who are fierce rivals on the pitch were united against the league's governing body. The ruling found that El Clasico was well known in Singapore as a commercially organised and promoted sporting property associated with La Liga rather than merely describing matches between the two clubs.

The dispute centred on an application filed in August 2022 featuring both club crests, a stylised 'C', and the words 'EL CLASICO' across goods including video game software, clothing, footwear, entertainment, sporting activities, and ticket reservation. La Liga opposed it in June 2024 with evidence of viewership figures ranging from 27,165 for a December 23, 2017 match to 68,384 for an October 28, 2018 match, plus two other matches drawing 56,361 in April 2021 and 60,521 in October 2021. The adjudicator gave limited weight to the clubs' evidence because it largely concerned use outside Singapore.

La Liga also won on similarity grounds, finding that consumers might mistake the proposed mark for an official variant of its existing marks given only minor differences in accent, capitalisation, and spacing. Represented by law firm Ghows, La Liga was awarded $10,500 in costs. A procedural wrinkle emerged when the clubs' legal representatives stopped acting in August 2026, leaving them without written submissions or representation at the hearing.

The adjudicator cautioned that his findings should not constrain future adjudicators where both sides fully argue the same issue.
items.title: Real Madrid and Barcelona Lose Singapore El Clasico Trademark Fight

Chinese shoppers are buying budget down jackets as cold weather arrives, with products priced below 500 yuan (S$97) selling briskly while consumers question the value of premium brands. A 399 yuan down jacket filled with 90% goose down made for Peking University sold out online in mid-November after drawing attention on Chinese social media, and a women's down jacket from US brand Rokka&Rolla priced at 499.9 yuan also sold out at Walmart-owned Sam's Club.

The trend signals more cost-conscious spending in a market where people have long been pushed toward luxurious clothing. Research firm iiMedia said the average price of a down jacket more than doubled over the past decade and was forecast to exceed 1,000 yuan in 2025, yet an November survey found jackets priced between 401 yuan and 600 yuan were most popular among consumers.

Bosideng, China's largest down jacket maker, has said the average price of its core products rose to about 1,500 yuan to 2,500 yuan. Mark Tanner, founder and managing director of Shanghai-based consultancy China Skinny, said many shoppers want comparable design or function without a large prestige premium rather than the cheapest copy.

The challenge is apparent for brands moving upmarket: Bosideng launched its third collection from British designer Kim Jones in November, but some higher-priced items saw limited sales on Tmall. A blue jacket advertised with brand ambassador Wang Leehom carried a price tag of about 2,278 yuan yet sold just 16 units over the 30 days to Nov 13.

Consumers are becoming more selective rather than simply trading down: Alibaba said more than 30 million down jackets were sold during 2026's Singles' Day festival, with Uniqlo and Bosideng ranking first and second by sales. Uniqlo surpassed 100 million yuan in Tmall sales within 24 minutes of promotions launching on Oct 20.

Demand remains resilient at the top end: Canada Goose said Greater China revenue rose 32.5% in the quarter ended September, and Moncler's chief corporate and supply officer Luciano Santel described China as a healthy region for its premium outerwear brand. Tanner noted that like every luxury brand, they will need to work harder than ever to justify their price points.

The contrasting performances reflect broader divergence in Chinese consumption: as economic uncertainty weighs on middle-class households through a property slump and weak wage growth, many are trading down or demanding greater value while wealthier shoppers continue spending on products offering quality, performance or status. Lv Jiaming, a 27-year-old factory worker in Shanghai, said he would not buy another jacket costing more than 1,000 yuan because there is little difference between one priced at 500 to 600 yuan and one over 1,000 yuan unless it is exceptionally good.
items.title: China's premium puffer jacket push meets consumer resistance

items.summary:
Sarah Wynn-Williams, the author of Careless People, argues that technology companies are using legal tools to suppress information about their most consequential technologies. She frames this as a modern form of censorship rooted in George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, drawing on the novel's 'memory hole' and her own experience living under a gag order while writing the book.

Wynn-Williams contends that control over narrative has become central to power in technology, achieved not by winning arguments but by leaving nothing contestable. She argues that NDAs function as private censorship enforced through arbitration and courts, noting that 'in libel, truth is a defence. Under an NDA, truth is the offence.' She observes these agreements are often signed at moments of maximum vulnerability for workers across many roles, creating what she describes as self-censored society without any physical furnace required.

She points to recent entertainment cases involving Russell Brand's conviction and David Walliams' denied allegations against young women, reporting that NDAs have been deployed in both instances. She notes these figures faced accountability while their professional standing was already diminished, expressing concern about powerful people benefiting from silence who deprive the public of information needed for warnings and accountability.

Wynn-Williams references an October 1945 essay by Orwell connecting weapons technology to political power, observing that expensive complex technologies concentrate power in few hands. She applies this reasoning to artificial intelligence, noting it requires tens of billions in investment from a handful of companies mostly concentrated in two countries, with most governments lacking resources to build such systems.

She reports that current and former employees at leading AI companies including OpenAI and Google DeepMind published an open letter two years ago requesting a right to warn. The letter asked for prohibitions on non-disparagement clauses and restrictive confidentiality agreements, anonymous reporting channels, and no retaliation against employees, stating some signed anonymously due to fear of various forms of retaliation.

Wynn-Williams states she has spent the most recent chapter of her career examining what happens when technology meets weapons Orwell warned about, noting AI is being integrated into weapons including command and control for nuclear systems. She raises the question of whether someone on the inside who saw something going wrong would be free to warn if they had signed away their rights.

She criticizes two decades of reacting to harms after they arrive rather than creating a vision for technology that serves society, arguing people cannot choose a different future without being allowed to describe the present. She concludes by acknowledging her own fear about potentially being crushed and bankrupted but urging readers outside the silence to remember what was suppressed, stating 'the thing about a memory hole: it only works if nobody outside it remembers what went in.'
items.title: Careless People author Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order and speaking out against big tech

items.summary:
Sony has begun giving retired Aibo robot dogs a second life in hospitals and other facilities through an adoption program that repairs and upgrades the units before redeploying them. The robots, which first went on sale in 1999, are no longer produced or sold, though Sony does not disclose how many have been donated or their pricing. Owners who parted with their Aibo reportedly donate the machines to Tokyo-based Sony Group Corp., where they receive maintenance and upgrades before being placed in new homes.

Yoshiyuki Katsuno, a Sony official overseeing the program, said owners often feel as though they are sending off a pet that has become like their own child. He added that Aibo encourages people to talk to one another and offers tired individuals something to lift them up, with hopes of spreading emotional healing and human interaction.

At St. Marianna University School of Medicine in Kawasaki on the outskirts of Tokyo, Dr. Manabu Komori of the otolaryngology department said a wandering Aibo had to be located during a recent visit but that the robot helps fill long waits for visiting patients and has persuaded reluctant children to get examined. He noted it motivates kids given how unpleasant hospital visits can be.

Komori pointed out that the hospital also uses real dogs, which require care, food, and can be temperamental, so he was careful not to claim robots are better than live animals. Jerry Wang, Executive Chairman of FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem in the United States, said cuteness is desirable in Japanese culture, where being 'kawaii' or cute is viewed as an endearing trait that encourages harmony and communication rather than weakness.

Wang added that if emotional attachment is sought, a cute shape works best whether it be a dog, cat, or even duck, contrasting with more foreboding-looking four-legged patrol robots offered by his company.
items.title: Sony Repurposes Retired Aibo Robot Dogs for Hospital Use

A zero-day vulnerability in the open-source network monitoring platform Cacti has been publicly disclosed, accompanied by a proof-of-concept exploit that lets unauthenticated attackers execute commands on vulnerable servers. The exploit, dubbed '4HTTP2SHELL' (previously 4HTTP2ROOT), was published Thanksgiving Day by cybersecurity researcher ek0ms savi0r of the Church of Malware, who demonstrated how it can be exploited using just four HTTP requests against a fresh session with no login or valid API key. The write-up, PoC exploit, and video were shared in a GitHub repository named 'Sad Girls 0day Club.'

The vulnerability stems from weak input validation that allows an unauthenticated attacker to inject SQL statements into the application's database and modify commands run by Cacti's real-time poller. RavenAI explains the attack abuses weak validation of guest users' graph display settings, letting attackers save malicious SQL in those preferences; when Cacti processes them it executes the injected SQL to alter the poller configuration and trigger OS commands. The exploit requires the Cacti guest account to be enabled but no valid credentials.

The researcher tested against Cacti Core 1.2.31, though it is unclear whether earlier versions are also vulnerable. watchTowr notes that privileges gained depend on which account runs the web server and poller processes; in many deployments this may be a low-privileged web server account rather than root, even though the researcher demonstrated full root access.

The vulnerability was not reported to Cacti before public release, prompting ek0ms savi0r to criticize how companies handle disclosures. Until a patch is available, administrators are advised to deactivate the guest account and restrict web interface access to trusted networks, review poller configurations for unexpected commands, and check logs for warnings about non-numeric values in graph display settings.

As of November 27 there have been no reports of exploitation. The text ends with an unrelated advertisement offering a free email security scan via Adaptive Security's AI agents.
items.title: Unpatched Cacti Zero-Day With Public PoC Gives Remote Code Execution

Volkswagen opened orders for its new ID. Buzz Beach, an electric van aimed at camping and overnight stays, beginning this week in the UK. The vehicle brings a retro-new take on the classic Type 2 microbus with modern technology and a flexible cabin, and Volkswagen said it 'brings adventure into the electric age.'

The camper sleeps two people using a removable bed frame and a folding mattress measuring about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m). The bed tucks away in the trunk for the five-seat layout, while it is stored vertically behind the third row of seats in the six- and seven-seat configurations.

For longer stays, Volkswagen added an Overnight mode that uses the battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous off-grid climate control. Other features include blackout curtains throughout the cabin, ventilation grilles on the front side windows, a standard 230V power socket adaptor for charging devices or running camping equipment, and a hidden foldable table and chairs set.

Pricing in the UK starts at £53,955 excluding VAT, roughly $71,000, rising to about $86,500 once VAT and on-the-road costs are included. Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles is offering financing from £555 ($726) a month with a deposit of £6,500 ($8,500).

The van will not come to the United States; VW delayed the ID. Buzz's return until the 2028 model year after introducing a similar Tourer variant for the 2027 model.
items.title: Volkswagen launches electric ID. Buzz Beach camper in the UK

items.summary:
Zoomlion arrived at bauma China in 2026 with more than 60 new-energy heavy equipment models spanning eight product categories, from driverless excavators to cabless loaders and hybrid-electric mining trucks. The company presented the display as evidence of its manufacturing strength and positioned itself as a leader in what it calls 'physical AI.'

The main attraction was a cabless Zoomlion excavator robot built around RobotOps, an embodied AI operating system based on a vision-language-action model that uses multiple sensors to provide a 540-degree view of the surrounding environment. The company said this wider field of perception is better than standard 360-degree camera views and lets the machine identify objects under various conditions.

According to Zoomlion, its Zbrain platform has been trained on millions of hours of operational data and tens of thousands of real-world scenarios so that autonomous machines can interpret natural-language job instructions. The system reportedly breaks complex tasks into step-by-step workflows before scanning terrain, classifying materials, and calculating digging and gripping paths for fully automated excavation, loading, slope dressing, brick paving, or material handling.

The company also brought examples of the Z01 and Z03 humanoid robots to guide visitors through its display. Zoomlion said these bipedal units build a new equipment asset roughly every six minutes and reportedly use facial and gesture recognition while performing interactive gestures such as fist bumps and waves.
items.title: Zoomlion Displays 60+ Electrified, AI-Powered Machines at bauma China 2026

The EPA's airborne chemical-detection program, known as ASPECT (Airborne Spectral Photometric Environmental Collection Technology), has largely stopped responding to emergencies after a decline that began in early 2021. According to Floodlight reporting by Inside Climate News, the single-engine Cessna responded to only seven emergencies since then, and former scientists say two of those—the February 2023 East Palestine train derailment and the August 2025 Smitty's Supply fire—were badly mismanaged.

The program once flew nearly 80 emergency missions over more than two decades. In its first two decades it averaged roughly four flights a year, but in the past five years that average dropped to about one flight per year. Floodlight attributes much of this decline to staff departures during President Donald Trump's first administration: the EPA required program personnel to relocate to Texas or face termination in 2019, and key scientists left without being replaced by experienced airborne-detection experts.

The plane also can no longer perform its core function. In June, an EPA Inspector General found that chemical-monitoring data now takes about a week of manual analysis instead of the designed five minutes. The agency blamed aging sensors and awarded Telops a $1.7 million contract for replacements expected to be integrated by early to mid-2027.

Former program scientists dispute this fix, arguing the old sensors still work and that EPA lost its initiative and expertise rather than hardware. Chris Manning, an infrared spectrometer expert with no ties to any party involved, said the new Telops sensors would complement but not replace the older instruments because they are slower, less sensitive, and poorly suited to moving targets.

The Smitty's fire response drew particular criticism: EPA reports posted nine days after the August 2025 explosion declared air safe, though a later analysis of raw flight data obtained by whistleblower Robert Kroutil identified high concentrations of neurotoxicant toluene and carcinogens trichloroethylene and naphthalene. An EPA manager acknowledged in a May 2026 email that some target chemicals may have been present but not flagged at the time, possibly due to sensor deterioration.

The East Palestine derailment response was also scrutinized: ASPECT did not miss the vent-and-burn operation initially because its services were requested more than two days after the February 3 disaster, and it collected only eight minutes of chemical data when it finally flew over. An EPA Inspector General investigation found errors including poorly documented procedures.

The decline comes as accidental chemical releases grow: the U.S. Chemical Safety Board tracked 133 in one year, up from 83 in 2021. The Trump administration is also proposing to roll back federal safeguards against chemical disasters.
items.title: EPA's Chemical-Detection Plane ASPECT Falls Out of Service Amid Sensor and Management Failures

items.summary:
OCCTO announced the results of Japan's 30th utility-scale solar procurement, allocating 27.7 MW against a target of 91 MW under its feed-in premium scheme for projects of at least 250 kW.

Eight qualifying projects totaling 41.4 MW submitted bids, but only seven totaling 27.7 MW were awarded support. The lowest bid came from Marushin Koei's 500 kW project at JPY 5.00 ($0.031)/kWh, while the highest bid of JPY 9.60/kWh was set by Machiokoshi Energy and Solar Field 13 for projects near 20 MW and 1.3 MW respectively; Solar Field 13 also won two additional 1.99 MW projects at JPY 7.50/kWh each, with the remaining bids landing at JPY 6.99/kWh and JPY 9.50/kWh.

The weighted average final price reached JPY 9.13 ($0.057)/kWh, marking a second consecutive rise in prices during fiscal 2026 alongside a second straight decline in awarded capacity. For context, the prior auctions allocated 38.2 MW at an average of JPY 8.89/kWh and 89.2 MW at JPY 6.74/kWh.

The exercise was the third procurement event in fiscal 2026. METI confirmed in March that it would end auction-based support for large-scale solar after fiscal 2026 while keeping incentives for smaller installations, and authorities proposed four categories of commercial projects eligible for continued priority support. Separately, ANRE set Dec. 11 as the deadline for new FIT and FIP certification applications for solar systems of 10 kW or more seeking approval in the current year.

The government is also shifting public support toward emerging technologies, prioritizing perovskite over conventional silicon with plans to deploy roughly 20 GW of perovskite capacity by 2040.
items.title: Japan's 30th solar auction allocates 27.7 MW

Companies are increasingly downplaying their environmental commitments through greenhushing rather than exaggerating them as in greenwashing, a trend that is growing among U.S. firms amid concerns about political, legal, and financial risks tied to publicly communicating sustainability goals. According to Prof. Ricardo Rüther of UFSC and Prof. Andrew Blakers of ANU, this restraint does not necessarily signal reduced corporate environmental action; instead it reflects a shift toward prioritizing implementation over public promotion even as renewable energy becomes more cost-competitive.

Academic research on U.S. publicly listed companies found that higher levels of greenhushing correlate with higher subsequent abnormal stock returns, suggesting investors may value demonstrated environmental performance over promotional communication. A 2025 survey by The Conference Board reported that 80% of surveyed sustainability executives were adjusting their ESG strategies in response to the new U.S. administration.

The authors note that PV module costs have fallen to about 5% of what they were 15 years ago, and battery prices are now roughly 9% of their 2010 levels, making renewable generation and storage more economically attractive while reducing companies' incentives to publicize such investments. They argue the industry's competitive bottleneck is shifting from equipment affordability toward grid connection capacity and integration challenges like reverse power flow, substation limits, power quality, protection systems, metering, and grid management.

The authors contend that customers increasingly want comprehensive performance solutions combining engineering, software, operations, warranties, financing, and clear financial returns rather than individual components. They warn that without integrating planning, market structures, and execution, solar expansion risks creating valuable assets in the wrong locations, while noting this trend unfolds against a backdrop of political uncertainty highlighted by failed COP31 negotiations in Antalya.

The authors frame greenhushing and declining PV and battery prices as two sides of the same market transformation, where companies can capture economic benefits without publicly promoting their sustainability commitments. They conclude that competitive advantage will increasingly depend on how effectively firms deploy, manage, and monetize solar and storage assets rather than how much capacity they install.
items.title: Greenhushing and Falling Solar Prices Shift the Industry's Bottleneck to Grid Access

Romania's Environment Fund Administration (AFM) closed a six-day public call on November 25 offering grants to household prosumers who want to add battery storage, with the program budgeting RON 400 million (EUR 75 million). Nearly 57,000 applicants responded and requested RON 803.5 million overall, making total requests about two times higher than the available budget.

Beneficiaries can receive up to 75% of their investment value but no more than RON 15,000 (EUR 2,800) each including VAT; AFM is grading applicants by proposed capacity and own contribution. Minister of Environment, Waters and Forests Natalia Intotero said the program supports household investments that give families greater control over consumption and bills while helping balance the energy system.

The initiative follows a rapid rise in solar prosumers: at end of September there were 394,868 prosumers including 357,148 households with 2.27 GW of solar power, per Romanian Energy Regulatory Authority (ANRE) data. Households operated 151,404 battery systems versus 5,144 for legal entities at that time.

The number of prosumers is reported to have surpassed 400,000 and may be near 400,000; the Association of Prosumers and Energy Communities in Romania (APCE) claimed last week it exceeded 200,000 with 2.2 GW of power capability.
items.title: Romania Allocates EUR 75 Million for Household Battery Storage

Iraq is negotiating with OPEC for permission to raise its oil production ceiling, according to Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair. He argued the country needs a higher quota to develop its energy infrastructure, and the request comes ahead of Sunday's OPEC+ meetings on 2027 production policy.

Three sources told Reuters that OPEC+ members have agreed in principle to leave their quotas unchanged for the first quarter of 2027, though this is not yet an official decision. Iraq currently holds a quota of 4.431 million barrels per day and wants its future allowance calculated against a production capacity of 6 million bpd. A third-party agency contracted by OPEC+ instead pegged Iraq's capacity at the more conservative figure of 4.9 million bpd, which would give Baghdad considerably less leverage in negotiating.

Iraq's push follows reported pressure from Washington to leave OPEC altogether; Reuters reported that U.S. officials encouraged Iraq to consider quitting earlier this year. Iraq's prime minister reportedly raised the possibility at a government meeting, but the Oil Ministry objected and favored negotiating for a bigger quota instead. The US State Department said its discussions with Iraq focused on energy infrastructure rather than membership.

Washington also reportedly encouraged Venezuela to consider leaving, though that country is currently exempt from OPEC production quotas and would not face immediate restrictions if it did so. Should both countries leave, they would join the UAE, which departed in May after years of disagreements over its own limits. Losing another major producer would reduce OPEC+'s market clout.
items.title: Iraq Pushes OPEC+ for Higher Oil Quota Ahead of 2027 Meeting

Ranbir Kapoor's mythological epic Ramayana: Part 1 reached a net collection of Rs1,000 crore in India on day 23 of its theatrical run, even though daily collections had fallen below Rs10 crore at that point. The film also stars Yash and Sai Pallavi.

Despite the slowdown, Ramayana overtook Baahubali 2's lifetime worldwide collection as reported by trade figures. Its global gross is now stated to have hit Rs1,790 crore, prompting questions about whether it can catch up to Dhurandhar 2, described as the only other Bollywood film to reach this milestone in 2026.
items.title: Ramayana crosses Rs1,000 crore as Ranbir Kapoor film eyes Dhurandhar 2 lifetime

British soft toy brand Jellycat, founded in 1999, is seeing a surge in adult buyers as part of the wider 'kidult' movement, with grownups purchasing items traditionally aimed at children. On Monday, London's Harrods opened what it calls a first-of-its-kind dining destination: a Jellycat cafe serving brunch made from edible and soft toy forms, including a peach granola bowl-shaped plushie that diners can eat.

Research by Circana found 'kidult' toy sales in the UK grew 22% in the first half of 2026, with one in five toys now bought by over-18s. At Nordstrom, the average age of a Jellycat buyer is 27, and the brand's revenue jumped 43% on the previous year to £450m according to October figures. The toys typically cost between £20 and £40, though rare versions can fetch upwards of £500 secondhand.

Audrey Tang, a chartered member of the British Psychological Society, describes Jellycats as 'tactile, comforting, calming and very cutesy' and dismisses age-regression concerns as judgment often rooted in parental messaging. She credits shared interests at events like Harrods with building community for those who may feel lonely or shy.

The brand's popularity is reflected in its ranking fourth among the UK's most-searched terms between January and September 2026, per eBay, alongside rising reports of shoplifting to resell. Celebrities including Bill Nighy, Sarah Jessica Parker, and Kylie Jenner have publicly embraced Jellycats, while collector Rachel Dyer, who began collecting in 2025, now owns 95 plushies.
items.title: Jellycat's 'kidult' boom drives Harrods cafe and surging sales

Budget retailer Poundland has gone into administration after its US-based owners, Gordon Brothers, rejected at least two solvent bids and declined to provide further funding. Administrators AlixPartners were appointed on Wednesday and have until Sunday for about six interested parties, including Martin Property Group, Zachert Private Equity, Xyra Group Holdings, and Dubai's Premier Quality Foods, to bid; many watchers expect the group of 600 stores in the UK and Ireland to be broken up. Kelvin Blake, a Birmingham shop-floor worker with 25 years' service, said Gordon Brothers 'punched us in the guts,' while other staff felt the collapse was inevitable.

Gordon Brothers reportedly collected close to £20m in interest payments and fees since buying Poundland for £1 last year and sits near the front of the creditor queue on a £30m shareholder loan. The retailer is short of funds, stocks are running low as suppliers have stopped sending goods fearing non-payment, and about 2,000 suppliers will take a considerable hit; one confectionery supplier Byxa said he was owed £68,515.20 while another clothing supplier cited more than $1.2m (£915,000) tied up in goods stuck in port.

The impact extends to Poundland's two distribution centres and head office, with nearly 300 people understood to work at its eight-hectare (19-acre) site in Bryn near Wigan that opened in 2018. Jo Welbourne of the Usdaw union described staff as 'absolutely devastated,' while a Gordon Brothers spokesperson said Poundland had faced several years of instability and cited £85m in new finance provided by its owners.

Shoppers across high streets expressed sadness at the prospect of closure, with some noting they would have to turn to larger supermarkets where prices are higher. In Woking, views ranged from those who loved the affordable store to shoppers who rarely visited; one worker noted it was not surprising given that many items can be bought online and delivered.
items.title: Poundland enters administration as Gordon Brothers rejects bids

items.summary:
An international team of marine geologists using a remotely operated vehicle called Jason/Medea found evidence of the deepest-known explosive volcanic eruption on Earth, located as much as 4 miles (6,500 meters) below the surface near Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench. The ROV observed and collected pyroclastic rocks composed of ejected rock fragments and volcanic glass along a forearc structure spanning 340 miles (550 km), with 10 dives total, seven of which occurred around Challenger Deep and three in shallower waters near Guam due to weather conditions.

Lead author Robert Stern described the discovery as recent igneous activity unprecedented at such depth, noting that pyroclastic rocks are well known from land and shallow ocean but not previously found this deep. The trench forms part of a subduction zone where one plate dives beneath another, with surface volcanoes typically located about 125 to 185 miles (200 to 300 km) away rather than within the trench itself.

The collected rocks contained broken rock and volcanic glass cemented in finer-grained material that Stern called unmistakably a product of eruption, though no active vent was found. The age remains unknown but appears recent geologically, and researchers are investigating how explosive eruptions occur at these depths given the intense water pressure, which Stern said makes the eruption style different from land or shallow-water volcanism.
items.title: Marine Geologists Find Deepest-Known Explosive Volcanic Eruption Evidence in Pacific Trench

items.summary: Work and pensions minister Pat McFadden said on Friday that there is no evidence so far that any personal details were compromised in a cyber incident which prompted his department to take some services offline. Asked whether the incident was a malicious act, McFadden described it as a 'serious cyber incident' and added that the investigation remains ongoing.
items.title: UK Pensions Minister Says No Evidence Personal Data Compromised in Cyber Incident

台文中描述韩度经济的快速拉升，强调它像中国一样正处于兴起之中，并指出“大而贫”的史典联系正在结束。

韩度2025年人均GDP达10,039美元（PPP永续2021国际美元），ev1/dt2/dt3），约为1990年水平的五倍，dt4。这一水平与中国2009年期相同，dt5，而韩度相比中国仅慢约15年，即从朱小麗1978年改革到韩度1991年取照，dt6/dt7。

韩度目前增长速度超过中国，ev8，人均GDP增长6%，生活水平每12年翻一倍，另约15年可达到人均20,000美元的中等收入国家，ev9。

极端贫困已大幅下降，从1993年的47.5%到2011年的27.1%，ev10/dt11/dt12，再到2023年的2.6%，ev14/dt13/dt15，采用世界银行3.00美元/日（2021 PPP）线ev16/dt17。

日常生活也发生改变：电力供给率从2000年的四成人降到2024年的99.9%，dr18/dt19，无间便认减从73.2%降到6.7%，ev20/dt21/ev22，孤儿死亡率自1990年以跌72%从84.4降到23.3，年均寿名提升14年至72.2死ev23/dt23。

文中提醒，韩度仍需改善就业与土地市场、空气、法院与国家能力ev24/dt24，并注意中国2009年同样面临许多问题ev25/dt25。

文任指出，世界九大国家已无但仍分为低收入，dr26/dt26，仅长士尼亚（排第十）仍属低收入层ev27/dt27，但自1990年以来人均收入已增加一倍以上ev28/dt28。

文任认为，史上“大耀”仅是少数小国早接西方资本主义的历史意外，ev29/dt29，而非原因关系ev30/dt30；今日正回到“差距不再驱动人口”的史典状态ev31/dt31。

items.summary:
An OECD and African Union report argues that African countries could strengthen their economies by borrowing more, provided the funds are directed toward productive projects. The researchers estimate that an extra $93 billion of investment over five years would generate more than 13 million jobs and add almost one percentage point to annual continental growth.

The report stresses a key caveat: how borrowed money is used matters greatly because African governments currently spend, on average, nearly one in four dollars raised as revenue on interest payments. It suggests the extra borrowing could pay for itself if spent wisely, pointing to Southern Africa's mining-related infrastructure as an area where new funds might be most effective.

Alongside increased borrowing, the report calls for debt deals to be fully disclosed and for improved debt management.
items.title: OECD-African Union Report on Borrowing

items.summary:
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Friday (Nov 27) in Kuala Lumpur that Malaysia's lawsuits against Google over alleged failures to address harmful online content will not affect the US tech giant's investments in the country. The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission sued Google for US$146 million on Wednesday, prompting concerns about whether the case would disrupt plans to invest billions of dollars in data centres and other infrastructure.

Anwar defended the legal action, saying Google had been slow to respond to complaints, with some left unanswered for up to half a year. He cited cases of online gambling that were reported but saw no action taken after six months. The MCMC alleges that YouTube failed to adequately address online gambling, scams and fraud on its platform and did not take proactive action against harmful content published by a controversial local blogger.

Google announced this month plans to invest US$15 billion in Malaysia over the next two years to build data centres and other infrastructure, expanding on a US$2 billion investment disclosed in 2024. The country is Southeast Asia's fastest-growing hub for new data centres, which house servers that train and run AI tools such as chatbots and image generators.

Anwar said he had spoken with Google's President and Chief Investment Officer Ruth Porat on Thursday, reporting that she told him Google would cooperate to address the issues. Malaysia has previously taken action against other major social media platforms, including TikTok, over allegations they failed to remove content deemed 'grossly offensive.'
items.title: Malaysian PM Says Lawsuits Won't Deter Google Investments

items.summary:
OpenAI filed counterclaims against Apple on Friday in federal court in San Jose, California, accusing the iPhone maker of pressuring suppliers to avoid its devices and using unfair employment agreements to keep talent from leaving. The filing also alleges that Apple stole OpenAI's trade secrets, turning an earlier lawsuit brought by Apple into a two-way dispute over intellectual property between the companies.

The legal conflict has overshadowed OpenAI's separate bid to sell its own products, which would place it in direct competition with Apple. Former Apple design leader Jony Ive is helping develop this product line, beginning with what is expected to be a doughnut-shaped smart speaker.
items.title: OpenAI Accuses Apple of Pressuring Suppliers and Stealing Trade Secrets

items.summary:
Pete Edochie, celebrated for his role as Okonkwo in the 1987 television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's novel Things Fall Apart, died on 25 November at age 79 in Enugu after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer. Joy Nnamdi said he was the perfect choice to bring the character to life and described him as 'the ultimate tough man,' rarely seen laughing despite his deep voice and commanding presence that made him an enduring embodiment of patriarchal authority on screen.

Born 7 March 1947 in Zaria, Edochie studied journalism and television in the UK before joining the Eastern Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation in 1967. He joined the pro-separatist Voice of Biafra during Nigeria's civil war, describing those years as 'the greatest personal challenge' he ever faced amid hunger and hardship. He later switched to acting over a decades-long career that bridged home-video productions and global streaming platforms.

His work reached wider audiences through MultiChoice's Africa Magic channels across the continent and via Lionheart (2018), Netflix's first original Nigerian film, as well as his 2017 Ghana comedy John and John. His contributions were recognised in 2003 when he received the Member of the Order of Niger honour.

In recent years Edochie gained an unexpected online following as social media users turned his distinctive expressions into memes conveying disbelief or exasperation, introducing his work to younger Africans while some who grew up watching him recalled being scared by his occultic and villain roles. Sani Muazu said parents in Kano would invoke 'Okonkwo will come and visit you' to keep children in check.

Tributes poured in after his death from fans, fellow actors, and President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, who described the loss as significant for Nigeria's film industry and cultural heritage. Actress Genevieve Nnaji called him a 'chosen one,' while Patience Ozokwor remembered him as an elder figure of wisdom.

His son Leo Edochie said his father's most important legacies were telling the truth and remaining honest, describing him as living an exemplary life worthy of emulation. Two of his six children, Yul and Linc Edochie, followed into Nigerian film, though some of the actor's endearing moments came when he let his guard down.

In 2021 he made a brief appearance in music star Phyno's video for 'Highway,' surprising fans with dance moves that revealed a lighter, more playful side to the septuagenarian behind his formidable screen persona.
items.title: Nigeria's 'ultimate hard man' actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79

items.summary:
A documentary titled Heal offers what is described as the most intimate look yet into Princess Catherine of Wales's private life, including how her cancer affected her physically and mentally. The film will broadcast on BBC TV on Sunday (Nov 29), ahead of airings in the United States on NBC, Australia on Channel 9, and Canada on CTV and Noovo.

Catherine, 44, wife of Prince William, is shown crying as she listens to messages from her three children during a charity challenge to scale Britain's three highest peaks within 24 hours. She told her brother James Middleton that the recordings would give her 'the reason to get out of hospital' and 'finish this challenge.' The climb involved Scafell Pike in England, Ben Nevis in Scotland, and Snowdon in Wales, a feat she completed in June to raise money for The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity.

Catherine said in March 2024 that tests following major abdominal surgery had found an undisclosed form of cancer after it was revealed her father-in-law King Charles also had the disease. She is now reported to be in remission after a course of chemotherapy. In voiceovers and clips from meetings with other cancer sufferers, she described being confronted by her own mortality as 'very hard' and characterized hospital time as dark, disorientating, and frightening.

She said the project's aim was to give something back to those who cared for her while helping others navigate life with cancer. Catherine acknowledged that her story differed from others and could not reduce 'the grief and pain that so many face,' but expressed hope that viewers would be reminded they are not alone and that beauty and joy can still be found even in difficult times.
items.title: Princess Catherine's Cancer Documentary 'Heal' to Air on BBC

items.summary:
A government-funded clinic in Sweden, Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened as what its doctors describe as the first facility worldwide dedicated solely to reassessing people who hold autism or ADHD diagnoses. The service is driven by young adults like Freya, 12 at referral time and now seeking a police career, whose original diagnoses they came to question once those labels became barriers to employment in Sweden's military, police, train driving and piloting roles.

Clinic lead psychologist Sebastian Lundström says the approach focuses on present-day functioning rather than past history, adding a note of reassessment without erasing the original diagnosis. He cites a small peer-reviewed study of 72 participants in which roughly 80% did not meet diagnostic criteria, while noting that all attendees already wanted to lose their diagnoses and so are unrepresentative.

Critics warn the service could deepen stigma by framing neurodiversity as something undesirable or fixable. Navid Ghannad of Autism Skåne argues these are lifelong conditions whose symptoms can resurface later in life, leaving people without support if reassessed away from their diagnosis. Advocacy figures including Jenny Hedin and Eric Donell contend the focus should be on changing employment rules rather than removing diagnoses.

The clinic is open only one day a month and serves locals; during its first year of operation some 400 to 500 people spoke with Lundström about reassessment. Requests from applicants in the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have been turned away as the service currently does not accept international patients.
items.title: Sweden Opens World's First ADHD and Autism Reassessment Clinic

items.summary:
At least 22 cassowaries have been killed on Queensland roads in 2026 so far, according to figures from the Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation. That figure is almost double the between-11-and-13 road deaths recorded each year since 2022 (ev1, ev2), with dt3 confirming the reference period as 2026 and ev4, ev5 noting the prior annual range of 11 to 13. Tropical Vets director Graham Lauridsen described a cluster of fatalities earlier this year, occurring roughly one per week for about six weeks (ev1). The rise may partly reflect better reporting and a healthier population after several years without major cyclones, though Lauridsen said that is not grounds for halting protection efforts.

Cassowary advocates are pressing the state government to roll out AI road signs following what they describe as a successful trial. In July 2025 (dt7), the Department of Transport and Main Roads announced a three-month test on the Kennedy Highway at Kuranda that achieved 97 per cent accuracy in identifying birds and a 31 per cent decrease in fatal strikes, figures drawn from the department's account (ev8, ev9). Afterward, the Cassowary Recovery Team identified five road-strike hotspots for potential sign installation. Liz Gallie of Mission Beach Cassowaries said locals expected signs to be deployed next at these sites but expressed frustration that nothing has happened since; in correspondence seen by the ABC she wrote to a minister in September and received an October reply stating more trials were needed but no plans had been made, with her own words emphasizing 'we just need it at Mission Beach' (ev10).

A TMR spokesperson said investigations are ongoing into how AI signs could be incorporated into ongoing cassowary-safety work, but noted that no further funding has been allocated and no trials are planned. The government is instead continuing a community awareness program, including two static roadside billboards on the Bruce Highway near Tully and Innisfail to encourage drivers to slow down (ev1). Jax Bergersen of the Kuranda Conservation Community Nursery said everyone in the Cassowary Recovery Team was frustrated after high hopes for the signs. Lauridsen added that AI signs avoid driver complacency associated with static signage, help mitigate conservation costs, and are especially timely now that hatching season has ended and chicks are on the road.
items.title: Cassowary advocates push for AI road signs after deaths nearly double

items.summary:
As rain fell at the grand final, North Melbourne defeated Melbourne by 56 to 52 on Friday night (7 Nov) to complete a historic three-peat in the AFLW. The piece notes this is their third consecutive premiership and that for the first time since 2023 they lost a game during the season, with challengers coming closer than in prior years.

North Melbourne won by dominating three phases of play. In the opening quarter Tess Craven kicked the first goal within 21 seconds and captain Jasmine Garner added a second six minutes later; both came off stoppage rather than turnover as they had done against this opponent previously, with Garner recording seven disposals, four inside-50s and the goal in that term.

Melbourne then shifted to a kicking game in the second quarter, producing their only two goals of the match from intercepts while posting 39 kicks to North Melbourne's 14 handballs. The Demons recorded a pressure factor of 2.30 across that quarter before rising to 2.38 in the third term, yet North Melbourne held its lead and turned the middle quarters into an arm's-length stalemate as intercepts from Garner (eight), Ash Riddell (seven) and Amy Gavin Mangan, Jenna Bruton and Eliza Shannon (all six each) helped drop Melbourne's kick rate to 50 per cent.

A five-minute burst in the last quarter turned a six-point lead into a 26-point victory. A long rebounding kick unlocked North Melbourne's speed, leading to a stoppage inside-50 and a goal from Bella Eddey that put them up by 13 points before Blaithin Bogue added two more goals for the comprehensive win.
items.title: North Melbourne Win Historic AFLW Third Consecutive Premiership

items.summary:
Three people familiar with the matter said hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, known as Cloud One, in an intrusion that could jeopardize sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

The breach was discovered within roughly a month during work to upgrade the system, according to two of those sources, and has since caused disruption across the platform. Reporters were unable to establish the identity of the attackers, determine the full scope of the intrusion, or confirm whether any data had been stolen.

In response, the Air Force issued a statement declining to comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems, while asserting that it continuously takes prudent measures to protect Department of the Air Force information, systems and mission capabilities.
items.title: Hackers Breach U.S. Air Force Cloud One Platform

items.summary:
The purse of Se Nah Park, a 24-year-old woman swept into the ocean at Panther Beach near Santa Cruz three weeks ago, was found Wednesday by a beachgoer at 4 Mile Beach south of Panther Beach. The Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office confirmed that Park had been caught in powerful waves on 8 November while attempting to return through the 'keyhole' archway after gathering around a bonfire with five others; four members tried to make their way back, and three reached safety up the cliffside before being struck by another wave. According to her friends' GoFundMe page, Park did not survive.

Park's body has still not been located as record high king tides affected the west coast during the discovery. The U.S. Coast Guard suspended active search efforts on 9 November after Lt. Max Holloway stated that extensive searching had exhausted available resources and environmental conditions complicated recovery attempts; his statement offered condolences to Park's family.

Despite the suspension, Park's family and friends have continued their own search efforts in the weeks since. Her supporters shared a message expressing hope 'that Senah can be found and brought home to rest,' noting that finding her purse may help bring them closer to locating her body.
items.title: Purse of California Beach Victim Found After Three Weeks

items.summary:
Schools in England are set to be required by Labour's proposed national curriculum reforms to allocate time each day for primary pupils and several days a week for secondary pupils to read for pleasure. Education Secretary Lucy Powell is expected to announce the measures, which include a statutory reading test at year 8 and an emphasis on whole books rather than excerpts, as part of efforts to tackle declining literacy rates and rising screen time. Powell told the Times that falling reading levels represent 'a ticking timebomb' for future generations while noting that reading should also be enjoyed by every child.

Powell is also expected to announce programmes of study for England's curriculum, which could include shorter exams in some GCSE subjects such as history, geography and modern foreign languages. Shadow education secretary Laura Trott welcomed the reforms but said they must accompany a serious effort to reduce classroom screen time. A July education committee inquiry recommended extending the National Year of Reading into a national decade and called for a reading guarantee ensuring all children have regular opportunities to enjoy reading.

Research cited in reporting found that reading enjoyment among UK children had fallen to its lowest level in two decades, with a sharper decline among teenage boys while girls' levels remained stable or improved. A survey by the National Literacy Trust reported that 39.1% of girls aged eight to 18 said they enjoyed reading in their free time compared with 25.7% of boys.
items.title: England Schools to Set Aside Time for Pleasure Reading

items.summary:
A discussion examines whether China seeks to overturn the international order, noting that some Western countries increasingly accuse Beijing of doing so as it rises. In response, China maintains that it upholds the basic norms of international relations enshrined in the purposes and principles of the UN Charter.

Vijay Prashad, Director of the Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research, argues that China's efforts are focused on developing itself while creating opportunities and benefits for others. He says what China seeks is a world of peace and prosperity.
items.title: China Engages Debate Over Whether Beijing Is a Disruptor to International Order

items.summary:
A study published in Electoral Studies by Josh Goddard at University College London finds that whether a Spaniard owns or rents their home has become the strongest demographic predictor of voting for center-right parties, outweighing occupation, income, education and age. The research analyzed more than 80 elections across 14 established Western democracies since 1985. Comparing two people with identical sociodemographic characteristics, Goddard estimates a homeowner has a 42% probability of voting center-right versus 28% for a renter, while the likelihood of voting radical left rises from 5.9% to 10.6% among renters.

The gap is narrower elsewhere: renters are only slightly more likely than homeowners to vote social democratic (28.5% versus 25%), far right (9.5% versus 8%) or Green (7% versus 5.5%), with almost no difference among social liberals (4% versus 4.1%). Goddard attributes this to support for those parties being driven more by education, age and occupation than housing tenure.

The divide sharpens when examining the type of rental property and kind of home owned: renters in social housing lean left while owners of high-value or mortgage-free homes favor center-right, with differences among homeowners based on property value exceeding the overall homeowner-renter gap. Across the 14 countries studied, a statistical index measuring the strength of the housing-voting relationship rose from 0.16 between 1985 and 1994 to 0.20 in 2015 to present, which Goddard links to rising home prices, mortgage spread and commercialization of rental housing after the 2008 financial crisis.

In Spain specifically, a 2024 CIS study found homeowners were almost nine percentage points more likely than renters to have voted for the center-right Popular Party (PP), while one in five renters supported Sumar versus just over one in ten homeowners. Researchers Álvaro Sánchez-García and Hugo Marcos-Marne at the University of Salamanca reached similar conclusions, finding that neighborhoods with rising rents shifted right when homeowner-heavy and left where renter populations grew, benefiting Unidas Podemos.

Public concern about housing has surged: according to CIS polling, the share listing housing among Spain's three biggest problems rose from 3.2% in October 2019 to 55.7% by October 2026. Goddard notes social democratic parties have historically held less clear-cut positions on housing but may now attract more renters as the radical left weakens, while Marcos-Marne warns that Vox's new public-housing priority policy could either broaden its appeal or risk alienating traditional voters ahead of the November 29 election.
items.title: Homeownership Now the Strongest Predictor of Spanish Voting

items.summary:
Euronews' weekly show Europe Tonight featured Javier Martínez-Cantó, a Research Fellow at the Spanish National Research Center, to examine how Spain's major parties plan to address housing and immigration ahead of Sunday's snap general election. The discussion centered on these two issues as they dominate the campaign.

According to the latest polls cited in the program, the results could unseat Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, potentially allowing a new right-wing coalition to take power instead. Martínez-Cantó also addressed what signal Sánchez would send to the rest of the European Union if he were able to remain in office.
items.title: Spain's Snap Election: Parties' Housing and Immigration Proposals

items.summary:
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for November 29 after months of political stalemate, and polls suggest the conservative Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox are improving on their 2023 result. The decisive question is whether they can clear the roughly 47% vote share needed for an absolute majority in Congress; current polling puts them at around 49%, leaving a margin of just two percentage points.

In 2023, PP and Vox won 45.4% of the vote and 170 seats, six short of an outright majority. The most consistent driver of any rightward shift is defection from the left: about 9% of PSOE's 2023 voters now say they will back PP or Vox, joined by roughly 4% of former Sumar voters according to polling firm 40dB., which on its own would lift the bloc above the threshold. But the right also faces leakage as around 200,000 people who voted for them in 2023 now intend to support Se Acabó la Fiesta (SALF), costing nearly one point and leaving PP-Vox right at the edge of a majority.

A second shift involves returning voters: those who abstained or backed minor parties in 2023 but will vote this time, and polls suggest they lean toward the right. This group accounts for roughly half of the bloc's advantage, adding around two percentage points to its combined total, though it is also the least reliable flow since many may stay home again.

Demographics offer little help either way: deaths have removed about 1.4 million adults who were more likely to back PP or PSOE than Vox or Sumar, while roughly 620,000 newly naturalized citizens vote much like the electorate as a whole. New voters—about 1.6 million young people too young in 2023 but eligible this time—are somewhat right-leaning and could add a couple of tenths of a percentage point.

The bloc's combined support has narrowed from 50.7% to 49.3% since the election was called, with most of the decline over the past two weeks, yet an outright majority remains the most likely outcome at five times out of six in their estimates. In a scenario where polls hold and turnout materializes, PP-Vox would reach around 49% and roughly 190 seats; if those shifts fail to play out as expected—mirroring 2023—they could fall to about 46%, hovering near the 176-seat threshold where the left's concentration in PSOE territory lets it convert votes into seats more efficiently. The difference between these outcomes amounts to just three voters out of every hundred.

The analysis draws on polling from firm 40dB., Spain's statistical bureau (CIS), and its own model, which assumes turnout around 75%, nearly five points higher than in 2023, though it notes the reliability of these voter flows remains uncertain.
items.title: Spain's election hinges on right-wing vote share

items.summary:
After eight years of socialist-led government, Spain faces a crossroads as it heads into Sunday's snap elections. Europe correspondent Richard Werly joined Angela Diffley to examine the final days of campaigning and the generational divisions shaping the vote. The youth are split between the left and the far-right Vox party, while Sánchez has campaigned heavily on housing and social issues.

Werly described Sánchez as a 'Teflon politician' who may see an outgoing prime minister perform better than expected at the polls. The broader question raised concerns whether Spain could witness the conservative Partido Popular making way for the far right into national government for the first time since the end of Franco's 40-year reign.
items.title: Spain's Snap Election: Sánchez, PP, and Far-Right Vox

items.summary:
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna confirmed in Baku that Estonia will close its border with Russia on 1 December, saying the move is needed to respond to growing security concerns and secure Europe. He noted that Estonia has faced an increase in Russian sabotage and attacks targeting European countries, though he added his country was not happy about closing the border.

Tsahkna opened Estonian embassies in Baku and Yerevan as part of a broader effort to strengthen ties with the South Caucasus, describing Azerbaijan cooperation as well calculated and long-term. He highlighted shared interests between the two nations across energy, digitalisation, AI, technology, tourism, education, and trade.

During his visit he stressed that developments in different regions are interconnected after arriving directly from Kyiv, where Ukraine had endured heavy ballistic missile attacks on the previous night. Estonia will co-host next year's Ukraine Recovery Conference with Ukraine, and Azerbaijan has reportedly provided assistance exceeding $50 million (€45.6 million), with its first humanitarian shipment of food and medicine arriving right after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
items.title: Estonia to Close Border With Russia on December 1, FM Says

items.summary:
EU Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius warned that proposed cuts to the bloc's next long-term budget could jeopardize major European defence and space projects. He said member states and institutional leaders are proposing to cut their initial proposal by 30 percent, or €40 billion, which he described as one of the biggest reductions across all spending lines of the Multiannual Financial Framework (ev1). Kubilius cautioned that this shortfall could prevent implementation of common-interest defence projects and space initiatives such as Iris Square and the Earth Observation Governmental Service (EOGS) due to a lack of funding at European level.

Kubilius framed these cuts against what he said is Russia's rapid military buildup, noting Moscow plans to raise its defence-military budget up to €180 billion (ev3), which he described as 30 percent more than it spent this year (ev4). He added that using purchasing power parity comparisons suggests Russia will spend around €500 or €550 billion next year, roughly matching combined EU member state spending (ev5, ev6). On drone production, Kubilius said Russia is producing around 10 million drones this year (ev7), with Ukrainians currently matching that figure but predicting Russian output could reach 20 million drones next year.

Kubilius credited the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence loans programme as a key boost to European defence, calling it 'really very successful' and noting a second call is underway to encourage member states to scale up production for Ukraine. He highlighted an industrial challenge in which delivery dates on contracts presented to Ukraine are typically 2028 or 2029 rather than 2027 (dt10), prompting efforts to incentivize faster, larger-scale European manufacturing.

Separately, Kubilius reacted to German reports that Russia is considering launching a nuclear-armed satellite, which Moscow denies. He said such weapons would be very dangerous because they could destroy space systems crucial for civilian life and security, underscoring the need to defend those systems against adversaries.
items.title: EU Defence Commissioner Warns Budget Cuts Threaten Major Projects

items.summary:
Burundi's Independent National Electoral Commission rejected opposition leader Agathon Rwasa on Friday for a false declaration, having registered as an independent candidate while remaining a party member. The commission approved seven of the ten applicants it reviewed, and those turned down have two days to appeal before the Constitutional Court. Rwanda's ruling CNDD-FDD party is expected to field President Evariste Ndayishimiye in the May 3 general election for his second term; he submitted his candidacy papers earlier this month with a deposit of 100 million Burundian francs ($33,000), which opposition parties argue is designed to keep them out. The final candidate list will be published on December 6.

Exiled civil society activist Pacifique Nininahazwe said the disqualification was 'no surprise,' describing it as part of a political elimination process aimed at neutralising Ndayishimiye's primary rival, who previously lost to Rwasa in the 2020 polls. The CNDD-FDD won all 100 seats in the National Assembly elections held earlier this year, which also saw irregularities reported.

Ndayishimiye has led Burundi since June 2020 after his predecessor Pierre Nkurunziza died; the government is seen as balancing between liberalising and cracking down on opposition. Rights groups and the United Nations have criticised human rights breaches in the country, including an 'alarming increase in extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances' flagged by the UN Human Rights Council in October.
items.title: Burundi Bars Main Opposition Leader From Next Year's Presidential Election

items.summary:
Mark Ian Cook, an avian ecologist heading the South Florida Water Management District's Everglades Research Group, uses low-flying helicopter surveys to photograph nesting colonies and wildlife in southern Florida. He tracks how wading birds respond to CERP, a federal-state effort authorized by Congress in 2000 that aims to return freshwater from Lake Okeechobee across the River of Grass into coastal Everglades and Florida Bay after decades of drainage reduced it significantly (ev4). Photos are his most reliable way to tally colonies holding tens of thousands of nests, he told Mongabay. His best frames also help persuade water managers by turning data into images that hold attention longer than graphs.

Wading birds respond quickly to water levels and historically supported more than 200,000 nests along the coast in the 1930s and early 1940s before canals caused coastal nesting to collapse (ev6). South Florida recorded a record 138,834 wading bird nests in 2018, with surveys dating back to 1995, and nests topped 100,000 again in 2021. Other species are rebounding too: American crocodile populations are increasing, waterfowl returned in concentrations not seen in roughly 80 years in 2024, and hunted-out American flamingos have come back as wintering birds.

Progress has been uneven though. After exceptional seasons in 2018 and 2021, wading bird nesting declined for several consecutive years, with drought contributing to the lowest levels recorded in roughly 30 years at Everglades National Park in 2025 (dt21). Rising seas have cut Florida Bay's roseate spoonbill nests from about 400 in 2012 to 157 in 2022, even as the birds established new colonies farther north. A severe drought spanning into 2026 underscored the birds' sensitivity to water fluctuations (dt3).

Storage remains a bottleneck because managers release much of Lake Okeechobee's excess water to coastal estuaries without room to hold it; the Everglades Agricultural Area Reservoir, built to store and send that water south, is due for completion in 2029. New bridges along the Tamiami Trail are making a difference anyway: about 10 times more water flowed beneath the road from January through July 2026 than in the same months of 2015 despite a harsher drought (dt23). That water moves toward the coast, helping keep Florida Bay's salinity low enough to avoid repeating the 2015 seagrass die-off. CERP is projected by its most recent report to Congress to take about 50 years at a cost of $26.9 billion in 2023 dollars.
items.title: Mark Ian Cook documents Florida Bay recovery as Everglades restoration restores freshwater

items.summary:
French media group Canal+ is targeting subscriptions in at least half of African households with access to television, as it expands operations following its acquisition of South African pay-TV giant MultiChoice. The ambition comes as the company seeks to tap into Africa's growing population and rising demand for locally produced entertainment.

Speaking at the launch of Canal+'s training academy in Johannesburg, David Mignot, CEO of Canal+ Africa and MultiChoice, said local productions remain central to the group's strategy, noting that thousands of hours of content are produced annually in local languages. He stated: 'Today, we produce 10,000 hours of scripted content—series, dramas—every year...and in around thirty languages.' Mignot added that African-produced channels consistently rank among the top three for audience impact across most countries where they operate.

Grace Loubassou, Canal+'s Sustainability Director for Africa, said the training investment aims to strengthen local talent and give African stories greater international visibility. She emphasized: 'We want these stories to be told by Africans themselves...to reach a global stage.'

Canal+ acquired MultiChoice in September 2025 (ev1), adding around 14 million subscribers from English- and Portuguese-speaking African markets (ev2) to its existing base in French-speaking Africa. The combined group now has approximately 23 million subscribers across the continent, making Africa a major part of its global growth strategy.

With competition from international streaming platforms intensifying, Canal+ is betting that locally produced stories, accessible distribution, and investment in African creative talent will help secure its position in the continent's rapidly evolving media market.
items.title: Canal+ Targets Half of African TV Households After MultiChoice Acquisition

visual.alt: Bar chart. MultiChoice subscribers added (Sept 2025) 14,000,000 subscriber; Combined group total across Africa 23,000,000 subscriber.

items.summary:
In Kaohsiung's Ciaotou district, a community is fighting an urban development project that threatens a 154-hectare (380-acre) woodland surrounding the former Ciaotou Sugar Refinery. After failing to find politicians to support their fight, they turned to an 83-year-old former factory worker nicknamed Forest Grandma to defend the woodland, which provides habitat for local wildlife and helps protect the area from flooding.

Chiang Huang-nu is running as an independent candidate in Taiwan's local elections on Nov. 28 with a campaign slogan of 'Vote for trees, not parties.' The push for development is tied to the growth of the semiconductor industry in southern Taiwan, with the project set to convert around 227 hectares (561 acres) of land into commercial and residential zones.

The woodland contains about 100,000 trees according to local environmentalists. Environmentalists warn that removing the trees would threaten habitats for fireflies and at least eight protected bird species in Taiwan. The National Land Management Agency said a significant part of the wood is considered artificial forest rather than natural forest, though it does not say how many trees will be felled.

Chuang Chieh-jen chairperson of the Forest City Association noted that residential units built for around 76,000 people in previous phases remain largely unoccupied. Chuang said Kaohsiung's population has been declining for 10 consecutive years and pointed to projections by the National Development Council that Taiwan's population could fall from 23.2 million in 2026 to 12.15 million in 2075.

Chiang Yao-hsien, Forest Grandma's son, said he estimates she could receive between 2,000 and 5,000 votes, a remarkable achievement for an independent candidate though it may not be enough to gain a seat.
items.title: Taiwan Community Pins Hope on 'Forest Grandma' to Save Beloved Woods

items.summary:
Gambia votes on December 5 in a presidential election that takes place nearly 10 years after voters ended the 22-year rule of military ruler Yahya Jammeh. President Adama Barrow, who succeeded Jammeh in 2017, is running for a third term despite an earlier pledge not to do so.

Barrow faces United Democratic Party leader Ousainou Darboe and other candidates, including youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda, independent Almameh Gibba backed by Jammeh, and former Vice President Isatou Touray. The race unfolds under the 1997 constitution adopted during Jammeh's rule; a proposed replacement with presidential term limits was rejected by the National Assembly in July 2025 after failing to secure the required three-quarter majority.

Barrow defends seeking another term, telling reporters that voters decide whether he should serve for a third time. He says he supports term limits but argues their introduction depends on securing enough parliamentary backing for a new constitution. Opposition parties say their focus is not only defeating Barrow but also ensuring the election is conducted fairly; United Democratic Party administrative secretary Lamin Manneh emphasized the Independent Electoral Commission's responsibility to guarantee credible, free and fair elections.

Analyst Malang Faye said the incumbent appears already ahead after the campaign period began on November 16, though he cautioned that rally attendance does not necessarily reflect ballot-box support. Many voters cite jobs, cost of living and public services as top concerns; the World Bank projects economic growth of 5.3% in 2026 while extreme poverty is expected to remain at about 21%. The 2025 Labour Force Survey puts youth unemployment at 11.5%, with 41.3% of young people not in employment, education or training.

The Independent Electoral Commission says 1,146,474 people are registered to vote across 53 constituencies, 730 polling centers and 1,773 polling stations, while it trains officials on voting procedures. A European Union election observation mission is deployed under an invitation from Gambian authorities, and the United Nations has urged candidates to honor a peace pact signed on November 16 that commits presidential candidates to respect the IEC's independence and seek redress through lawful channels.

The December 5 election will test not only Barrow's bid for another term but also whether the democratic gains made since 2016 can be translated into lasting reforms and improved living conditions. Faye noted the campaign is still taking shape, with some parties yet to begin campaigning.
items.title: Gambia's December election tests Barrow's third-term bid

Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of Informer TV in Serbia, was arrested on November 25 on suspicion of causing panic and disorder through the media and obstructing justice after urging police to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June 2025. Authorities say his broadcasts created an atmosphere they described as public lynching, labeled 97 citizens enemies of the state, called protesters scum, hyenas and vultures, warned of a bloodbath and civil war, showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air, and ran wiretapping claims presented as conspiracies. The prosecution alleges that between 2023 and 2026 he systematically used the channel to incite hatred against activists, independent journalists and political opponents of the previous government.

The arrest comes amid Serbia's transition after the Student List won the late October parliamentary election and ended the Serbian Progressive Party's 14-year rule. Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation called Vucicevic a propagandist and weapon in Aleksandar Vucic's hands, citing threats against prosecutors and judges, accusations that journalists plotted to assassinate the president or sell out Kosovo, and a secret 'Viewer Intelligence Service' she said filmed people secretly. She noted more than 1,000 court cases over reputation brought against Informer, with courts upholding claims in 92% of those concluded over three years.

Informer's parent company Insajder Tim reportedly received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 through procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding. Representatives of the Student List claimed state-owned Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month, though Telekom cited business confidentiality when asked for details.

Vucicevic's defense says the proceedings punish speech and blur freedom of expression with criminal liability. He has been remanded in custody for 30 days; the offense carries six months to five years' imprisonment. Stevanovic said Serbia may be meeting its human rights obligations, but warned the outcome is uncertain because the executive branch, police and Ministry of Interior remain under the outgoing government until a new cabinet forms, raising questions about whether this reflects an internal power struggle or manipulation.
items.title: Informer TV editor Vucicevic arrested over June protest broadcasts

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned a drone attack on Kuwait that killed two Italian nationals and injured four others, warning that renewed hostilities in the region could have 'devastating consequences' for the Middle East and beyond. The attack occurred on Nov. 26, with a UN statement delivered Friday by spokesperson Stephane Dujarric confirming that the assault also left a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national among those injured.

Guterres expressed solidarity with Kuwait, extended condolences to the families of the deceased, and wished the wounded a speedy recovery while urging all parties to exercise restraint. He reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable path toward lasting peace, stressing the need to prevent further escalation amid what he described as increasingly fragile regional stability.
items.title: UN Chief Warns of Devastating Consequences After Drone Attack on Kuwait

The UN's search for a new secretary-general continues even as Antonio Guterres approaches his departure next month, with the Security Council unable to reach consensus after nine rounds of straw polls. Former U.S. Ambassador Robert Wood told NPR that it is too late and unlikely anyone would enter the race now given global turmoil; he sees the contest mainly between Rebeca Grynspan, Rafael Grossi, Carolyn Rodrigues-Burkett, and Lana Nusseibeh, though Nusseibeh faces activist opposition over her country's support for a militia accused of atrocities in Sudan. Elizabeth Cousens, president of the UN Foundation, described the field as strong and capable while urging the council to rally behind one candidate before year-end, noting that all four top contenders have drawn opposition from at least two permanent Security Council members.

Analysts warn whoever is chosen will face a compressed timeline; Anjali Dayal compared it unfavorably to appointing someone in December for January. The State Department expressed interest in returning the UN to peace and security work rather than what officials called politicized ideology, while Dayal pointed out that the Trump administration did not use the UN against Iran and Russia violated the charter by invading Ukraine. Behind closed doors, experts say negotiations may involve horse trading, including promises of senior posts to permanent members to overcome veto threats.
items.title: UN Race for Secretary-General Continues as Guterres Term Ends

Turkish parliament speaker Numan Kurtulmus called on Friday for the creation of a new global system to address international crises and protect state sovereignty, arguing that the current order has failed to halt Israel's attacks on Palestinian territories. Speaking at the opening of the 12th Meeting of Speakers of Parliaments of the MIKTA group in Canberra, Australia, hosted by Australian Parliamentarians Sue Lines and Milton Dick, Kurtulmus attributed this failure to structural flaws within the UN Security Council that prevent any intervention regardless of global will.

Addressing a session titled 'Multilateralism, Parliamentary Leadership and Shared Responsibility,' he described an international system undergoing profound transformation amid growing geopolitical competition, polarization, and regional conflict. He characterized MIKTA's five member states as middle powers well positioned to build bridges between differences rather than form further blocs, emphasizing the group's capacity for parliamentary diplomacy in developing shared responses to global crises.

Describing nearly all institutions of the global system, particularly the UN, as being 'in a state of complete failure,' Kurtulmus urged MIKTA to help establish a fairer order based on human and sovereign equality. He cited the UN80 Initiative as an important first step while criticizing the international community's inability to resolve the Russia-Ukraine war or address Strait of Hormuz tensions, which he said are disrupting the global economy. Looking ahead, Kurtulmus outlined Türkiye's aim to strengthen MIKTA's role in economic development through trade, investment, connectivity, and cooperation among its five G20 members.
items.title: Türkiye's Parliament Speaker Calls for New Global Order Amid UN Failures

The Central Reserve Police Force has been deployed in Tamil Nadu's Thiruparankundram Hill near Madurai to oversee security and surveillance on Saturday, following a directive from the Supreme Court that the ceremonial Karthigai Deepam lamp be lit at the Deepathoon stone pillar atop the hill. The deployment comes ahead of the scheduled lighting ceremony at the Deepathoon.

Police personnel had already been stationed in the area near the Deepathoon before the CRPF arrived to reinforce security for the event.
